question.:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as $r(t)=8\cos t\,i+5\sin t\,j$ for $t\in[0,2\pi].$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186133897/plots/3b009e06d950eb7bfe07293e173d86927ce43d402d20633792507b6c73bee28f.png)
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and

$$\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=0-(-1)=1.$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D)&=\iint_D\text{d}A\\&=\iint_D(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y})\,\text{d}A\\&=\oint_C P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}$$

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$\oint_C P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-\oint_C y\,\text{d}x.$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$r'(t)=\langle -8\sin t,5\cos t\rangle.$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$\begin{aligned}-\oint_C y\,\text{d}x&=-\int_0^{2\pi}5\sin t\cdot(-8\sin t)\,\text{d}t\\&=40\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2 t\,\text{d}t\\&=40\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{1-\cos 2t}{2}\,\text{d}t\\&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left(20-20\cos 2t\right)\,\text{d}t\\&=\left[20t-10\sin 2t\right]_0^{2\pi}\\&=\left(40 \pi-0\right)-\left(0-0\right)\\&=40 \pi\end{aligned}$$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=-2t\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}y\,dx-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}y\,dx \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}1{t}^{3}\cdot (-2t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & =2[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2\left(\frac{1^{5}}{5}-\frac{(-1)^{5}}{5}\right) \\  & =2\left(\frac{1}{5}-\left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)\right) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
